name: Sara Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Sara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Of course. I'm Sara, I'm 27, and I'm the main tractor and combine driver on the Whitfield farm. It's about 400 hectares, mostly wheat, barley and oilseed rape, with a flock of sheep that grazes the stubble in winter.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Let's start simple. Walk me through a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: In autumn I'm drilling, which is sowing the seed, from first light until the dew comes down at night. In spring I'm spraying, and in July and August I'm on the combine, sometimes until midnight, with the grain trailers running back and forth to the store. The tractor already steers itself by satellite down the field, so my job is turning at the ends, watching the drill and fixing what blocks. I love harvest, the dust and the smell and finishing the last field. What wears me out is the weather, because one wet August can ruin a year's work.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's at home, and how do you use AI, if at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Tomas, my partner, who's a mechanic at the tractor dealer in town. We'd like to get married in a couple of years. I use AI now and then, mostly to identify a weed from a photo or check a spray label. We've got less than a month's money saved, and farm jobs round here don't come up often.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. We call this one AI Plateau.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me. Most of the new stuff is just a better version of the old stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool, like the autosteer, and no more. The work still needs someone who knows the land and turns up when the weather's right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved. I'm not scared of change, but I've seen enough sales reps promise the world at farm shows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am, and maybe use the weed app a bit more. Tomas and I would keep saving for the wedding and maybe a small house in the village.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like the forecast promising a dry week at harvest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd want AI to do that it can't now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A drill that would tell me when it's blocked before I've done half a field wrong. That costs us money every autumn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you push for anything at work in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. The Whitfields would still need me. I'd ask for more pay, because I've driven their combine for five harvests now.

S0.say: I'd say it's a useful tool, like the autosteer, and no more. The work still needs someone who knows the land and turns up when the weather's right.
S0.think: I'd be relieved. I'm not scared of change, but I've seen enough sales reps promise the world at farm shows.
S0.do: Carries on as now and uses the weed identification app a bit more. Saves with Tomas for a wedding and a small village house, and asks for a raise after five harvests.
S0.feel: Calm, like a dry forecast at harvest.
S0.quote: I'm not scared of change, but I've seen enough sales reps promise the world at farm shows.
S0.fieldNote: Sara already works with self-steering tractors and treats AI as the next tool. She is confident about her value to the farm. Her wishes for the technology are practical, like a drill that warns of blockages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. We call this one Steady Disruption.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one makes sense to me. Farming's always changed that way, bit by bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farms should adapt the way they always have, by trying things and keeping what works. I'd also say we need more apprenticeships, because the people who fix and run the new kit should come from farms, not from cities.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think driverless tractors arrive on big arable farms first, and that's us. The Whitfields might keep me as the person who watches three machines from a pickup, or they might not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the Whitfields to send me on any training for the new machines as soon as the dealer offers it. Tomas would tell me which machines actually work, because he fixes them. I'd save a bit more, and I'd learn to use the farm software properly over the first winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a practical way. Something to plan for, not lose sleep over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does having a mechanic at home change things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the good thing about Tomas. He sees which ones come back broken. If he says a machine is rubbish, I don't trust the sales talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you miss the driving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a bit. I like driving. Watching a screen all day isn't the same as feeling the combine bite into a good crop.

S1.say: I'd say farms should adapt as they always have, by trying things and keeping what works. We need more apprenticeships so the people who run the new kit come from farms.
S1.think: I think driverless tractors arrive on big arable farms like ours first. The Whitfields might keep me to watch three machines from a pickup, or they might not.
S1.do: Asks her employer for training on new machines as soon as the dealer offers it and checks with her mechanic partner which machines really work. Saves a bit more and learns the farm software over the first winter.
S1.feel: Uneasy in a practical way, something to plan for rather than lose sleep over.
S1.quote: Watching a screen all day isn't the same as feeling the combine bite into a good crop.
S1.fieldNote: Her partner's work as a mechanic gives her inside knowledge about which machines actually work, and she uses it to decide when to move. She stresses apprenticeships and people from farming backgrounds. Under the practical tone she would miss driving itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. We call this one AGI by 2028.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's two harvests. I'd hardly have time to blink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and communities need to stick together and help each other through it. I'd say the farms should stay with the families who farm them, not get bought up by investment funds with robot fleets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job's gone within two harvests. Grain is the easiest farming to automate, it's big flat fields and the same job over and over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back straight away and stop saving for the wedding, we'd do it at the registry office. I'd ask Tomas's boss if there's any apprentice work at the dealer, because someone will need to fix all these machines, at least at first. And I'd ask my parents about moving back in if it came to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach drops just thinking of it, like hearing rain on the roof in the middle of harvest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Tomas's job be safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a while, maybe. But if robots can do my job, I'm not sure they can't do his in a few years. That's what scares me, it's both of us on the same rope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd blame?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really. It's how markets work. I'd blame the government only if they made it worse by letting big funds buy all the land.

S2.say: I'd say families and communities need to stick together through it. Farms should stay with the families who farm them, not go to investment funds with robot fleets.
S2.think: I think my job's gone within two harvests. Grain is the easiest farming to automate, with big flat fields and the same job over and over.
S2.do: Cuts back at once and swaps the wedding savings for a registry office ceremony. Asks about apprentice work at her partner's tractor dealer and about moving back in with her parents if needed.
S2.feel: Alarmed, with a sinking stomach like rain on the roof at harvest.
S2.quote: That's what scares me, it's both of us on the same rope.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture threatens her partner's job as well as hers, which is what frightens her most. She blames markets for nothing but would blame government if it let investment funds buy the land. Family is her safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. We call this one AGI by 2031.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. All right, I can work with five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when apprenticeships matter. Young people should be learning to repair and run machines now, not in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is enough for me to become one of the people who keep the robots going. I'm good with machines already, I just haven't got the paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start an agricultural engineering apprenticeship at the dealer, part-time if I can, while still driving at harvest. We'd keep saving, even forty or fifty a week. And we'd get married in the second year, small, so we're settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a good way. Like before a big harvest, when you know it's going to be hard but you know what to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the robots fix themselves by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have a trade either way. A good mechanic can fix a dishwasher or a drone if she has to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does five years feel better than two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. Five harvests is enough to see which machines last. With two, I'd be guessing. With five, I'd know.

S3.say: I'd say this is when apprenticeships matter. Young people should be learning to repair and run machines now, not in five years.
S3.think: Five years is enough for me to become one of the people who keep the robots going. I'm good with machines already, I just haven't got the paper.
S3.do: Starts a part-time agricultural engineering apprenticeship at the dealer while still driving at harvest. Saves forty or fifty a week and marries Tomas in a small ceremony in year two.
S3.feel: Anxious in a good way, like the start of a hard harvest when you know what to do.
S3.quote: A good mechanic can fix a dishwasher or a drone if she has to.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets her steady approach work: see which machines last, then train for them. The apprenticeship fits her traditional values about learning a trade. She brings the wedding forward a little to feel settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. We call this one AGI by 2036.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. That's a lot of harvests.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to train people properly, and we should use it. I'd say farms should be helped to pass on to the next generation, with the skills to run them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is enough that I could end up with my own business. Tomas and me, fixing and running farm robots for the farms round here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the combine a couple more years and save, then start the apprenticeship around year two or three, once it's clear which machines are winning. We'd get married, have kids, and maybe buy a small yard for a workshop by year eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Hopeful, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you and Tomas actually talked about a business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've talked about it in the pub. He's the better mechanic, I'm better with the farmers. Ten years makes it a plan, not a dream.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you worry about having children in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I'd want to be sure the money's coming in. But I wouldn't put my whole life on hold for a machine.

S4.say: I'd say there's time to train people properly, so we should use it. Farms should be helped to pass on to the next generation, along with the skills to run them.
S4.think: Ten years is enough that I could end up with my own business. Tomas and me, fixing and running farm robots for the farms round here.
S4.do: Stays on the combine for two more years while saving, then starts the apprenticeship once it's clear which machines are winning. Marries, plans children and aims to buy a small workshop yard with Tomas by year eight.
S4.quote: Ten years makes it a plan, not a dream.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years she pictures a family business with her partner, built on his mechanical skill and her contacts with farmers. She keeps her family plans on track. This is a self-reliant answer that fits her traditional outlook.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it would take Tomas's job as well as mine, and we've got nothing saved. What would help is paid apprenticeships for farm people to learn the new machines, and rules that stop investment funds buying up the land.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about couples. A lot of people on farms are married to other people on farms, or to the dealer, or the vet. When farming changes, it hits whole households, not just one job.

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Thank you. I've got a drill to get back to.

headlineQuote: That's what scares me, it's both of us on the same rope.
portrait: Sara is a 27-year-old tractor and combine driver on a large grain and oilseed farm, living with her mechanic partner Tomas on less than a month of savings. She already works with self-steering tractors and uses AI now and then, and she believes in learning a trade, family and keeping farms in family hands. Under gradual change she waits for her partner's verdict on which machines actually work, then trains. The two-year picture alarms her most because it would hit both their jobs at once. With five or ten years, she plans an apprenticeship and imagines a robot repair business with Tomas.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI scenario, because it would take both her job and her partner's with nothing saved.
whatWouldHelp: Paid apprenticeships for farm people to learn the new machines, and rules to stop investment funds buying up farmland.
